steps.title: A pulse is not an error
steps.question: MsgReceive returns 0. What should this plain receive loop do?
steps.observation: The deliberately wrong <= 0 branch drops a pulse before its handler.
steps.diagnosis: MsgReceive returns -1 on error, 0 for a pulse, and a positive receive ID for a message. A pulse has no blocked sender to reply to.
steps.fix: Separate rcvid == -1, rcvid == 0 and rcvid > 0. Dispatch pulse codes only in the pulse branch.

steps.title: Receiving is not completing a message
steps.question: A client uses synchronous MsgSend. The server receives its message then forgets it. What is missing?

options.log: A server log line unblocks the client
options.complete: Complete the received request with MsgReply or MsgError
options.pulse: Reply to any unrelated pulse instead

steps.observation: In this scenario the client remains reply-blocked; printing received is not completion.
steps.diagnosis: The positive receive ID identifies a received message. MsgReply unblocks the client's send; errors can be returned with MsgError.
steps.fix: Give each accepted request an intentional reply/error path. Retain a receive ID only when deferring a reply deliberately; handle disconnect/unblock lifecycle separately.

steps.title: A resource-manager read is a bounded slice
steps.question: For this finite seekable /dev/edu result, the OCB offset equals the result length. What should the next read return?

options.eof: Return zero bytes (EOF) after validating the read

steps.observation: The wrong handler repeats 3628800 forever, so cat never reaches EOF in this finite-result design.
steps.diagnosis: Validate read access and message shape with iofunc_read_verify. Then apply the result bounds and per-open OCB offset. Verification does not implement your payload or EOF policy.
steps.fix: For this finite result: copy at most min(requested, length-offset), advance the OCB offset by bytes returned, and return zero at the end. Separate opens need separate OCB state; dup may share an OCB.

steps.title: An ability is not a pathname policy
steps.question: A process is allowed the required IO ability subrange. What has that established?

options.path: All clients now have access to /dev/edu
options.bounded: Only that ability operation/domain/range; not pathname authorization
options.all: Every privileged operation is now allowed

steps.observation: A successful ability setup alone cannot demonstrate a /dev/edu connect denial or allow.
steps.diagnosis: procmgr_ability controls identified process abilities, with operations, root/non-root domains and optional subranges. Resource access and loaded security policy are distinct evidence.
steps.fix: Specify the needed ability separately, narrow its domain/range, check return codes, and test deny/allow in separately authorized runs. Do not claim pathname policy without actual policy and access observations.

steps.title: Exit zero is not the device oracle
steps.question: Your edited EDU program exits 0 but writes 12345679 and reads edcba986. The required pair is 12345678 / edcba987. Which verdict is justified?

options.pass: PASS because exit code is zero
options.fail: FAIL the specified value oracle; fix the write, not the expected value
options.native: HOST prediction proves current native acceptance

steps.observation: The complement is internally consistent, yet it is the wrong operation for the specified exercise.
steps.diagnosis: Application self-report and stage oracle are different checks. This repeats the repository's historical wrong-edit lesson, not a new QNX execution.
steps.fix: Correct the operand to 12345678, retain the fixed expected value, rebuild and obtain separately authorized source-bound native evidence. Here only your reasoning is checked.
